subject: clockworkDog
pitch: A wind-up clockwork terrier made of polished brass and copper. Riveted body plates, visible gears turning in its chest, a big winding key on its back, springy jointed legs, floppy leather ears, glass-lens eyes with a green tint, a tail made of a coiled spring, and a little red collar with a brass tag.
reasoning:
I'm planning the dog's proportions and skeleton structure, sketching a terrier-like build around 0.45m long, with a spine chain running from pelvis through chest, neck, to head as the core joint hierarchy.

Now I'm setting up the legs and body mesh — a lofted sweep along the spine with varying width/height stations from rump to chest, giving it a tapered terrier silhouette, then adding a mottled brass paint finish for a weathered patina look before moving on to the chest gear window detail.

Working out gear orientation...

I'm mirroring the chest plate assembly for the opposite side and assigning the spine bone explicitly rather than relying on default joint proximity. For the riveted body bands, I'm planning small sphere rings as rivets around thin swept sections encircling the torso.

Since the body surface isn't a perfect circle, I'm using surface ray casting from a manual direction vector to get proper hit frames at each rivet position, then sticking small hemisphere geometry at those hits for bands positioned at three different z-heights along the torso.

Skipping null hits is fine since surface ray scanning is cheap. Now I'm designing the head and neck chain for the terrier: a boxy skull with long muzzle and beard, connected via a neck polyline from chest to head with named joints "neck1", "neck2", and "head" as the chain tip pointing forward.

Simplifying this — I'll keep the neck chain to two spans with a separate independent head joint attached at the tip, aimed forward, then sweep the neck with tapered radii. For the skull I'm scaling a low-poly sphere to form the cranium, then building the muzzle as a tapered box frustum extending forward from the face.

Adding the jaw next as its own joint parented to the head, with a tapered lower-jaw frustum, a dark bronze nose sphere at the tip, a few brass wire beard spikes under the chin, copper eyebrow bars, and small teeth details.

Now I'm designing the eyes: a green-tinted glass lens sphere with a brass torus rim, positioned symmetrically on the face and oriented to match the curvature of the cranium so the rims sit flush against the surface.

Next I'm working on the floppy leather ears, planning them as a teardrop-shaped flap hanging from a joint near the head, using a simple jointed chain so they drape down and outward in a natural resting pose.

Actually I realize the flat orientation needs the normal facing sideways so the ear is thin in that direction and wide vertically—setting the chain's up vector to point along x should give the right frame for a side-facing ear.

Next I'm adding a leather-brown ear color with a rivet trim and rounded caps, then working on the collar: a red torus ring wrapped around the neck, oriented so its axis aligns with the neck's tangent direction at that point rather than the default z-axis.

Now I'm adding a small ring loop for the tag attachment, then working on the winding key on the back of the body—a cylindrical shaft topped with a butterfly-shaped bow, extruding the wing outline in the XY plane.

Still writing butterfly key geometry...

Then I'm planning the leg rig: jointed springy legs with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints forming a chain for front legs, positioned symmetrically on the body.

I'm defining a coil spring helix for the lower leg using a spiral path with set turns and pitch, sweeping it thin and copper-colored, while keeping the upper leg as a rigid rod attached at the elbow joint.

For each leg I'm structuring capsule segments between shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw points, with brass ball joints at the elbow and wrist, a coiled spring plus a thin central rod for the lower segment, and a rounded foot shape at the paw.

Now I'm positioning the paw ellipsoid so its bottom edge touches the ground plane, adjusting joint y-values so the chain aligns properly, then moving on to set up the hind leg hip and knee coordinates mirroring the front leg structure.

For connecting segments at odd angles, I'm writing a helper that builds a spiral spring path between two arbitrary points—computing the direction vector, picking a perpendicular offset for the starting radius, and deriving pitch from total length divided by turn count so the coil wraps consistently along the bone's axis.

Defining hind leg joints now: hip, knee, hock, and paw positions per side with L/R naming suffixes, then setting up thigh capsule segments between hip and knee for each spring leg.

I'm checking for clashes between the gear window, shoulder plates, and hind plates along the z-axis, so I need to nudge the window center and verify body width stations stay clear at each z-slice.

I'm also sizing the hind plate and thigh capsule positions so they align with the narrower body width near the hip, adjusting the x-offsets slightly to avoid overlap while letting the thigh joint protrude naturally.

Now I'm thinking through whether to add visible gear clusters beyond the side windows — considering a chest cavity or front gear cluster but deciding to skip the glass dome idea and keep it simpler with side windows showing three gears each. I'm starting to write the function that generates the gear outline shape by alternating tooth points around the circumference.

Writing gear outline logic...

Checking gear-to-gear distances so the big, medium, and small gears mesh properly without overlapping, then adjusting their z/y positions slightly to get the spacing right. I'm also noting they stay at the same x depth since they're coplanar, with alternating brass/copper/gold tones, and planning a dark hub cylinder for each gear center.

Now turning to the tail: a coiled spring shape rising up and back from the rump, tapering in radius from base to tip across several turns, with a three-joint tail chain for animation.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton hierarchy: a pelvis root joint, a spine chain with two joints parented to it, and hind/front leg chains parented to pelvis and spine2 respectively, defining their start positions in local space.

I'm sketching the spine path points and reasoning through how the body loft stations extend past the chain's z-range, confirming the bone-span lookup still works since it only treats positions beyond the chain's end specially. I'm also setting up the head joint parented to neck2 at the end of the neck path.

Now I'm adding the head's associated features: ear chains parented to head, whisker spikes below the muzzle, small eyebrow shapes above the eyes, and a nose sphere positioned at the muzzle tip.

I'm shaping the muzzle as a tapered box from the face toward the nose, narrowing in width and height, with the lower jaw box sized and positioned to align its top edge with the muzzle's underside for a natural bite-line overlap.

For the cranium I'm using a scaled low-poly sphere with flat shading for a faceted look, pairing it with a shared brass material tuned to moderate roughness and low metalness for a polished but not mirror-like finish.

Now I'm anchoring the ears to the sides of the cranium and building out a brass/copper color palette, planning alternating riveted body plate stripes along the z-axis to give the body a mottled, segmented metal look.

Adding belly shading and seam band placement...

Placing larger rivet spheres directly on the seam bands instead, around 12 per band spaced via along(path), with outward direction computed from a per-segment center and bone assignment based on z-position. I'm skipping rivets on the plate faces, adding a small brass rivet at the ear tops, and considering a small gear detail on the forehead using an extruded plane with its normal derived from cross product of the facing axes.

Now I'm working out placement for gears near the back key mechanism — estimating the body's y-position at various z-stations to position a flange cylinder as the key base, a thin shaft cylinder rising to the bow, and a gear plate positioned just behind the key.

I'm also defining the key's joint attachment, choosing spine1 as the parent since its z-range covers the key's position, then starting on the bow outline geometry by sketching the right-side half-profile to mirror into a butterfly wing shape.

Confirmed non-self-crossing. I'll position the bow at y≈.42 so it spans just above the shaft, give it thickness with a beveled edge, and add small dark cylinder "holes" at the lobe centers as decorative dots for visual detail. The rest of the body—nose, mouth, tail, paws touching the floor—all checks out fine.

Now I'm composing the full code: importing builder utilities, setting up spring segments for both front (elbow-wrist) and hind (knee-hock) legs plus a central rod, and defining tuple types for coordinate vectors before writing out the brass material constant.

Building the joint and spine chain structure...

Still writing paint logic...

I'm adding a gold highlight on the top-facing surfaces, then simplifying the head, neck, and legs to plain brass tones. For the body, I'm lofting a tapered profile along the spine bone from rump to chest with varying widths and heights at each station, using the painted brass material across ten sides.

Checking clearances between the belly, hips, and legs confirms everything fits without overlap. Then I'm adding decorative copper seam bands by sweeping a small circular cross-section along loops traced on the body's surface at a few z-positions, binding them to the same spine chain for deformation.

Now I'm scattering small gold rivets along those seam loops, orienting each one outward from the body's central axis and binding them to the nearest spine bone so they move correctly with the body mesh.

Then I'm adding paired chest windows mirrored across the body's centerline, placing dark circular extrusions with a slight bevel near the upper chest, oriented so their outline plane faces forward in world z and anchored to the spine bone. I'm defining a ring-generating helper to produce the circular outline points for these windows and the gear shapes that sit alongside them.

I'm checking the math on gear radii and offsets so the big, medium, and small gears stay within the window's circular boundary without overlapping its edge -- adjusting the window radius and gear center positions until the distances between gear centers and the window radius work out consistently, since my first pass pushed some gears slightly outside the circle.

Now I'm adding hub cylinders at the gear positions, then starting to write a helper function to generate the gear tooth outline geometry.

Defining leg joint coordinates...

Adding joint spheres and rods...

I'm adding a gold bolt sphere outside the plate and placing the front and hind plate discs at their respective positions, checking that they sit properly against the body surface. Now I'm starting to write a spring helper function that builds a coiled wire shape between two points, computing direction, radius, and turns.

Finishing the spring function: I'm creating a perpendicular offset vector for the spiral, building a path around the axis using the spiral function, then sweeping a rounded wire mesh along that path with the given radius, color, and bone attachment. For the tail, I'm deciding to type the bone parameter more loosely to allow either a joint reference or a chain.

For the tail chain, I'm defining a polyline path from the base to the tip with interpolated midpoints, computing the direction along the tail, and sweeping a tapering spring shape (radius narrowing from .022 to .01, six turns) along it, with a copper mounting ball at the base and a small bead at the tip. I'm double-checking that the pitch times turns equals the total path length so the spring geometry closes correctly.

Now I'm moving to the neck: sweeping a tapered radius profile along the neck path, giving it a brass tone, and adding a collar torus positioned partway along the neck using its tangent and radius at that point so the torus sits flush on the surface.

Still working out the tag geometry...

For the tag I'm building a small disc with a ring attachment and a dark engraved detail, hung from the collar with a tiny torus link. Now moving to the head, I'm placing glass-lens eyes symmetrically with a slight scale flatten and a green tint for that glassy look.

I'm adding dark pupils and small white highlights inset into the lens spheres, plus a thin rim ring angled outward to catch the eye, and copper eyebrow boxes tilted slightly for a terrier-like expression. I'm positioning the cranium joint with a forward-angled direction to set up the head's base orientation.

Now I'm setting up the ear joint chains with a few segments going from base to tip, then sweeping a leaf-shaped profile along them using a radius function that widens near the base and narrows toward the point...

Placing beard spikes under the jaw with brass-dark bone color, angled downward and forward from the jaw bottom line. I'm skipping teeth since the mouth stays closed, and considering a thin dark box to suggest the mouth line gap between jaws.

Adding a small nose sphere scaled to be flatter and wider, positioned near the muzzle front in dark bone tone. For the forehead I'm placing a gold gear shape as decoration, extruded with a hub, oriented along the head's x-axis and rotated to face upward. Now moving to the key assembly, starting with a cylindrical stem bound to the key bone near the top of the head.

Adding a flange ring beneath the stem, then building the bow shape positioned slightly behind and above, checking that the bow's extruded outline aligns vertically with the stem so they overlap properly. I'm adding two small cylindrical holes through the bow lobes, dark colored so they read as cutouts, sized to slightly protrude past the bow's thickness for a beveled visual effect.

I'm deciding to skip the ear rivet sphere since the ear attaches close to the head anyway, and confirming the tail mount and other small details are already handled—gears and side windows are done, the head ears are correctly mirrored on the left side, and I'm double-checking that each part specifies an explicit bone reference so weighting doesn't default to nearest-joint guessing.

Defining joint chains...
